strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely under-explored problem: one-to-many Socratic tutoring in clinical medical education (ward-round style collaborative instruction), which is a meaningful departure from prior one-on-one tutors (SocraticLM, MEDCO).

The work presents a complete, coherent pipeline: ClinEdu (multi-agent simulator with decoupled patient scripts/personas and diverse student cohorts), ClinTeach (~48K Socratic teaching dialogues), and MedTutor-R1 (SFT followed by GRPO with a structured three-axis rubric reward including a veto mechanism). The design is well-motivated and clearly documented, with extensive prompts and training hyperparameters in the appendix supporting reproducibility.

Evaluation is multi-pronged: automated simulation-based redeployment, human expert evaluation (3 experts, 50 dialogues, Fleiss' kappa 0.79), a real user study, robustness analysis across heterogeneous student agents, and scalability analysis from 1 to 10 students. The scalability result (stable ~8.2 average score up to 10 students vs. a ~15% drop for baselines) is a notable and interesting empirical finding.

Ablations are reasonably thorough, covering the RL stage, each reward axis, the veto mechanism, base-model choice, and each simulation component (patient, specialist, supervisor), with results that are internally consistent with the claims.
The paper is generally well written, the rubrics (Tables 1, 7-9) are thoughtfully designed and could be independently useful, and an impact statement plus LLM-usage disclosure is included.
weaknesses: Evaluation circularity is a central concern. ClinTeach training data, the Socratic Steps used by the judge, and the evaluation environment are all generated within the same ClinEdu framework using the same persona/instruction conventions. A model fine-tuned and RL-optimized on this distribution is naturally favored when redeployed and judged in that same environment, so the headline results (e.g., matching o3/GPT-4o, +20% over the base model) may partly reflect distribution matching to the simulator rather than genuine pedagogical superiority. External validation is thin: the human expert study covers only 50 sampled dialogues.

The human evidence is underpowered and not statistically analyzed. The real user study involves only three medical undergraduates, yet the paper claims MedTutor-R1 is 'the definitive user favorite.' No significance tests or confidence intervals are reported anywhere for human evaluation, user study, or the LLM-judge comparisons against o3/GPT-4o, despite 'surpassing o3' being a headline claim; three-run standard deviations (~0.1) are presented but not tied to any inferential statistics.

Heavy reliance on LLM-as-judge for both reward and evaluation invites judge bias and reward hacking: the model is directly optimized against the same type of rubric-based judge (via GPT-4.1-style scoring) later used for evaluation. Clinical accuracy/safety (CS axes, MPS) are adjudicated entirely by LLM judges without verification against medical references or clinician validation of judge accuracy, which weakens the paper's central safety claims.

Potential data contamination: ClinTeach is built from the MedXpertQA training split while the 230-case test subset is drawn from the same benchmark; question decomposition and Socratic steps derived from the same question pool may leak reasoning patterns relevant to test cases. The paper does not discuss this.

Presentation and consistency issues reduce reliability: the code-release URL in the abstract is incomplete ('Code is released at' with no link); axis naming is inconsistent (Axis 2 'Analysis Quality' in Table 1 vs. 'SGA-1/2/3' in Appendix C vs. 'AQ-1/2' in Figures 22); Figure 23 is captioned 'analysis quality judgment' though it covers clinical safety, and references a nonexistent 'Axis 4'; the judge/generator LLMs for dataset construction are never identified; Table 3's VQA accuracy reporting is under-explained.

Several strong claims are under-supported or overstated: 'first multimodal Socratic tutor' is asserted without qualification; the claim that the simulator is 'high-fidelity' lacks any human validation of simulation realism (e.g., no expert assessment of whether simulated students/patients behave like real ones); and educational impact (whether students actually learn better) is not measured beyond 3-user Likert ratings.

strengths: The problem setting—Socratic, one-to-many instruction in clinical education via simulated ward rounds—is genuinely underexplored relative to existing one-on-one tutoring systems (SocraticLM, MEDCO, EduChat), and the paper articulates a plausible motivation for it.

The system is described in considerable engineering detail: agent role separation (patient, students, specialist, safety supervisor), the three-phase interaction protocol, the structured multi-tag reasoning format, and full prompts in the appendix support reasonable reproducibility of the pipeline.
The three-axis rubric reward with a veto mechanism for safety-critical criteria is a sensible design, and the rubric tables (ETS/MSM/MPS) are unusually concrete and behaviorally anchored.

The ablation study is fairly comprehensive, covering RL, the thinking tags, individual reward axes, the veto mechanism, and simulation-stage components (patient/specialist/supervisor agents, one-vs-multi-student).
weaknesses: The central evaluation is circular: both training data generation and evaluation occur inside the same ClinEdu simulator, with the reward signal produced by an LLM judge and the headline evaluation also produced by an LLM judge (GPT-4.1) using author-designed rubrics. The model is thus optimized on essentially the same signal it is later scored on, making claims like 'outperforms the base model by over 20%' and 'comparable to/surpassing o3' likely artifacts of judge alignment rather than evidence of genuine pedagogical superiority. There is no independent downstream measure of learning (e.g., whether simulated or real students actually learn more).

The claim that a 7B model beats o3 rests almost entirely on judge scores in the authors' own environment; the automated results actually show o3 (8.42) slightly above MedTutor-R1 (8.35) on MedXpertQA, so the 'surpasses o3' claim depends on a 3-expert evaluation of 50 dialogues—an extremely thin evidentiary basis for such a strong headline claim.

The real user study involves only three medical undergraduates, with no statistical testing, yet the paper asserts MedTutor-R1 is 'the definitive user favorite.' This is far too small to support any user-preference conclusion.

Internal inconsistencies undermine confidence: the main text describes a weighted-sum reward with veto set {CS-1, CS-2, IS-1}, while Appendix C says the final reward is 'the sum of all individual scores' with a -15.0 penalty and uses different axis names (SGA vs. AQ); the code release statement is a dangling sentence with no URL; the reward/eval judge model identity is vague ('powerful judge model'), leaving unclear whether the reward judge is the same as the evaluation judge.

The fidelity of the simulation itself is never validated: the 'personality-driven' patients and diverse student cohorts are LLM-generated archetypes, and there is no evidence that simulated student behaviors resemble real learners. Since both training and testing live in this unvalidated environment, conclusions about real-world teaching ability are speculative.

Evaluation against a ground-truth 'Socratic Steps' path that is itself LLM-generated raises further concerns about what the metrics actually measure, and the multimodal claim is only weakly supported (modest VQA gains, no analysis of image-grounded teaching behavior).

The 'first multimodal Socratic tutor' novelty claim is asserted without careful positioning against closely related simulation-tutoring systems, and the contribution is primarily an application of existing components (multi-agent simulation, SFT, GRPO, rubric rewards) to a new domain.

strengths: The problem setting is genuinely underexplored: one-to-many Socratic tutoring in clinical education with multimodal inputs, in contrast to the dominant one-on-one instruction paradigm (SocraticLM, EduChat, TutorRL). This is a clear originality point.

ClinEdu is a thoughtfully engineered multi-agent environment. The decoupling of the objective Patient Script from subjective Personas, the 300-persona databases for patients and students with documented construction prompts (Figures 8-16), and the three-phase interaction protocol with Specialist/Safety dual review are well-specified and would be genuinely reusable by others.

The three-axis rubric-based reward with a veto mechanism for critical safety/structure failures (Table 1, Eqs. 1-2) is a sensible and clearly articulated RL design, and the ablation table shows each axis contributes measurably.

Evaluation is multi-pronged: automated LLM-judge interaction evaluation on unseen cases, human expert evaluation with reported inter-rater reliability (Fleiss' kappa 0.79), a small real-user study, robustness tests across student models (Table 11) and class sizes 1-10 (Table 10), plus standard VQA benchmarks (Table 3). The scalability 'performance cliff' finding for baselines beyond 3 students is a concrete, interesting result.

Reproducibility is comparatively strong: full training hyperparameters (Appendix C), all agent/judge prompts included, code release promised, and the dataset construction pipeline is documented in enough detail to rebuild.
weaknesses: Evaluation circularity is the most serious concern. MedTutor-R1 is trained on ClinTeach data generated inside ClinEdu, with rewards scored by an LLM judge; it is then evaluated by redeploying it into the same ClinEdu environment, with GPT-4.1 as judge using metrics (ETS/MSM/MPS) that closely mirror the reward axes (IS/AQ/CS). The model is thus optimized for, and tested against, the same simulator and a same-family judge. The 'unseen cases' caveat does not remove this: the environment's dynamics, agent behaviors, and judging criteria were all part of training. No external, held-out evaluation environment or human-taught reference condition is provided.

The headline claims are weaker than stated. On automated MedXpertQA average, MedTutor-R1 scores 8.35 vs o3's 8.42 - it loses, and the 'comparable to o3' and 'surpasses o3' claims rest on the 50-dialogue human evaluation (8.64 vs 8.52) with only 3 raters. No statistical significance testing is reported anywhere in the paper despite the many small-margin comparisons.

The real-user study has only three participants. Claims that MedTutor-R1 is 'the definitive user favorite' from n=3 are not statistically meaningful, and the paper presents them with more confidence than the evidence supports.

There is no measurement of actual learning outcomes. The evaluation judges the tutor's teaching behavior (as scored by other LLMs and by expert raters watching transcripts), but never tests whether students taught by MedTutor-R1 learn more than students taught by baselines - which is the ultimate claim implicit in 'pedagogical effectiveness'.

Simulated students and patients are all LLM-generated. The paper does not validate that these LLM personas behave like real learners (e.g., against expert judgments of persona realism or actual student data), so conclusions about 'adaptive teaching to diverse students' are conditioned on LLM-simulated diversity.

Minor but notable presentation and consistency issues: the code URL in the abstract is empty; the appendix refers to 'Analysis Quality (SGA-1, SGA-2, SGA-3)' while the main text uses AQ-1/AQ-2; the abstract's '48K Socratic teaching dialogues' vs Table 5's 48,484 requires care; and the dataset is drawn from MedXpertQA train split while MedXpertQA is also an evaluation set, making the in-distribution advantage of the 20% improvement over the base model hard to disentangle from simple familiarity with the question distribution.

Given the medical safety-critical setting, safety guarantees rest entirely on LLM-based judges and reviewers; no analysis of the safety judge's false-negative rate or any red-teaming of unsafe outputs is provided.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: one-to-many (group) alignment for AI tutors, instantiated in clinical education with heterogeneous learner states and safety constraints.

Comprehensive multi-tier evaluation protocol: in-situ interactive simulation with multi-axis rubrics, human expert assessment (3 experts, 100 dialogues), a 200-participant real user study, controlled error-injection experiments, and cross-judge robustness checks (GPT-4.1, Gemini 3 Pro, GPT-5) that mitigate single-judge artifacts.

Well-designed RL reward: a decomposed three-axis rubric with a veto mechanism for safety/format failures, plus an unusually honest and useful Appendix D documenting observed reward-hacking behaviors (spoiler shortcut, sycophantic safety avoidance) and how the reward mitigates them.

Extensive ablations (removing RL, thinking, each reward axis, veto, individual simulation agents) and scalability/robustness analyses (group sizes 1–10; diverse student-agent models) that support the central engineering claims.

The simulator and training/evaluation prompts are documented in exceptional detail (Appendices F–K), and the limitations section is candid about simulator-to-reality gaps, vision scope, latency growth, and the short-term nature of the user study.

The structured <think_student>/<think_group> traces plausibly explain the observed scalability gains relative to baselines suffering context dilution, and ablation 'w/o Thinking' (7.94 vs 8.35 avg) partially supports this attribution.
weaknesses: Fundamental circularity risk: the model is trained on ClinTeach (generated by the ClinEdu simulator) and then evaluated in-situ within the same simulator, judged by an LLM against rubrics closely mirroring the training reward axes. ClinTutor-R1 may score well partly because its outputs match the simulator's distribution and the judge's format expectations, while baselines' 'performance cliff' may partly reflect distribution mismatch rather than true capability deficits. No out-of-distribution interactive evaluation (e.g., a second, independently built simulator) is provided.

LLM-judge dependence remains heavy: despite the three-judge robustness check (all LLM judges using the same rubric), the quantitative superiority over strong models (o3, GPT-4o) rests mostly on LLM scoring; differences are modest (e.g., 8.35 vs 8.42 for o3 on MedXpertQA average), and no confidence intervals or significance tests on these gaps are given.

Human evaluation is thin relative to headline claims: only 3 experts rating 100 dialogues, 'p < 0.05' is asserted without specifying the test; the reported κ = 0.79 is ambiguously attributed (inter-annotator agreement for the user study vs judge-human agreement) and κ is an odd statistic for continuous Likert ratings; the user study design (within- vs between-subjects, randomization, blinding) is undescribed, and IRB/ethics approval details are only generically stated.

The 'Theory of Mind' framing is overclaimed: the mechanism is structured chain-of-thought tags in prompts/SFT data, not a learned belief-state model; no ToM-specific evaluation (e.g., probing whether the model's <think_student> analyses are accurate against ground-truth student profiles) is conducted, so the interpretability/auditability claim is not quantitatively verified.

Data contamination and split hygiene are under-specified: both training (~4K) and testing (230 samples) come from MedXpertQA; it is unclear whether the 230 test cases were excluded from all pipeline stages (decomposition, script generation, dialogue generation) — the paper should state this explicitly.

The 'first vision-language agent' claim is weakly supported: the multi-agent evaluations appear predominantly textual, and Table 3's VQA generalization (e.g., 25.10 on MedXpertQA) is presented without clarity on the metric, its significance, or comparison to specialized medical VQA models.

The student/patient agents are themselves LLMs; claims of 'emergent group dynamics' and 'high-fidelity simulation' rest on prompt engineering without validation that simulated students behave like real learners (the 200-participant user study partially addresses this but participants rate only the tutor).

Several quantitative claims are internally loose: 'outperforms baselines by over 20%' and 'achieves parity with proprietary models' are averages over favorable metric choices; on MedXpertQA average, GPT-4o/o3 actually score higher or equal, and MPS is lower for ClinTutor-R1 than o3.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: one-to-many (group) instructional alignment, instantiated in a clinically grounded setting, with a clear articulation of the dual objectives (individual scaffolding vs. collective progress) and safety constraints.

The artifact suite is substantial: a configurable multi-agent simulator (ClinEdu) with decoupled patient scripts/personas and specialist/safety filters, a ~48k dialogue Socratic dataset, released prompts, training hyperparameters, and detailed rubrics (Tables 1, 8-10) that make the methodology inspectable.

The evaluation protocol is unusually broad for this area: automated in-situ simulation evaluation, multi-judge robustness checks (GPT-4.1, Gemini, GPT-5 in Appendix H), expert human evaluation, a 200-participant user study, scalability tests (1-10 students), robustness across heterogeneous student agents, and a controlled error-injection experiment with a defined metric (CSR).
The reward-hacking analysis (Appendix D: spoiler shortcut, sycophantic safety avoidance) and the veto-based safety reward are thoughtful and add value beyond the headline model.
The limitations section is candid (simulator-to-ward gap, static-modality scope of 'vision-language', latency scaling, lack of longitudinal learning-gain evidence).
weaknesses: Circular evaluation undermines the central claims. The model is trained (SFT + GRPO) on dialogues generated inside ClinEdu, with a reward defined by the same three-axis rubric (ETS/MSM/MPS) that is later used by the GPT-4.1 judge for the primary automated evaluation. Optimizing directly toward the test metric via an LLM judge makes the headline 'outperforms baselines by over 20% and achieves parity with GPT-4o' unreliable; structured outputs (XML think-tags, JSON) matching the reward format may itself be favored by the judge.

Apparent train/test contamination. The text states MedXpertQA instances were 'randomly sample[d] 230 instances each for testing, using the remaining ~4K for training' rather than respecting the benchmark's official splits. Since ClinTeach dialogues are built from these same QA pairs (including answers and decomposition steps), the gains on MedXpertQA (Table 3: 25.10 vs. 18.39 for the base model) could partly reflect memorization of the very cases tested. This needs a clean-split or held-out-source experiment.

Effect sizes are tiny and significance reporting is weak. Key 'wins' are on the order of 0.1 judge points (e.g., MSM 8.55 vs. GPT-4o's 8.39 on MVME; avg 8.35 vs. o3's 8.42 on MedXpertQA, where o3 is actually numerically higher). Std devs over three runs are reported, but no significance tests for the automated results; the p<0.05 claim in the human evaluation is unspecified (which test, which comparison).

The human evidence is thin relative to the claims. Expert evaluation uses only 3 raters on 100 dialogues; the 200-participant user study omits critical design details (within- vs. between-subjects, randomization, how the seven systems were presented, whether 'kappa = 0.79' is even the right statistic for Likert satisfaction ratings). Satisfaction ratings do not measure learning outcomes, and the paper concedes no longitudinal evidence exists.

Internal inconsistencies suggest insufficient care. The veto set is stated as {CS-1, CS-2, IS-1} in Eq. 2 but Appendix C applies the veto to IS-1, CS-1, CS-2 while Table 1's veto framing differs; Appendix C references an 'AQ-3' criterion absent from Table 1; the abstract/intro claims 'sub-5s latency up to 10 students' while the Limitation section admits roughly linear latency growth with student count needing future engineering fixes.

Overclaimed novelty and positioning. 'First vision-language agent for one-to-many alignment' is contested by MEDCO, SimClass, PEERS, and prior multi-learner tutoring work; the 'vision' component is largely decorative (static images only, as admitted), and the vision-only VQA comparison (Table 3) omits stronger open baselines like InternVL3.5.

Reference quality is poor and undermines credibility: the introduction cites Ma et al. (2025) (video motion transfer) and Ma et al. (2026) (FastVMT) as support for multi-user alignment, which are topically irrelevant, and several citations carry implausible 2025/2026 identifiers.

Reproducibility is currently not demonstrated: the GitHub link is empty and code/data are only promised 'upon acceptance'. Given that the entire evaluation depends on the authors' simulator, judge prompts, and data pipeline, this materially weakens verifiability.

Baselines are not trained/evaluated symmetrically: ClinTutor-R1 benefits from in-domain SFT data and a rubric-aligned output format, while Med-SocraticLM/TutorRL etc. are adapted differently, so much of the gap may reflect format and data advantages rather than the proposed ToM-style thinking mechanism. An ablation training the base model on identical data with only the rubric removed partially addresses this, but the thinking-mechanism ablation (w/o Thinking: 7.94 vs. 8.35) does not isolate format effects.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly framed problem: one-to-many alignment (teaching a heterogeneous student group) is a genuinely underexplored setting, and the clinical ward-round testbed concretely operationalizes the context-dilution / goal-misalignment challenges described in Figure 1.

Substantial end-to-end contribution: a multi-agent simulator (ClinEdu), a 48k-dialogue dataset (ClinTeach), and a trained tutor (ClinTutor-R1) with SFT + GRPO and a three-axis rubric reward including a safety veto. The reward-hacking analysis in Appendix D (spoiler shortcut, sycophantic safety avoidance) is a valuable and honest treatment of RL failure modes.

Unusually comprehensive evaluation: automated interaction evaluation with three independent judges (GPT-4.1, Gemini 3 Pro, GPT-5) showing stable rankings, expert human evaluation on 100 dialogues, a 200-participant real user study, scalability tests from 1 to 10 students, robustness across diverse student agents, and a controlled error-injection experiment (CSR). This multi-pronged validation goes well beyond a single LLM-judge table.

Thorough ablations (Table 2: w/o RL, w/o thinking, per-reward-axis removals, reward veto, LLaVA-based reward, single-student and agent-removal settings), which support the claimed importance of each component.

Reproducibility is taken seriously: full training hyperparameters (Appendix C), all judge/agent prompts in the appendix, released code URL, and explicit commitment to releasing code and dataset. The limitations section is candid (simulator realism, vision scope, latency growth, short-term user study).
weaknesses: Potential circularity in evaluation: both the training data (ClinTeach) and the primary automated evaluation are generated within the same ClinEdu simulator, with a GPT-4.1 judge scoring dialogues. The tutor was explicitly trained to produce the <think_student>/<think_group> structure and Socratic style that the judge rubrics reward, so part of the measured advantage may reflect format/style alignment with the judge rather than genuinely superior pedagogy. The judge-robustness check (Appendix H) mitigates judge-choice sensitivity but not this structural bias.

Margins over strong baselines are small: ClinTutor-R1's average scores (8.35 MedXpertQA, 8.49 MVME) are essentially at parity with o3 (8.42/8.45) and GPT-4o (8.36/8.47), with differences within reported standard deviations. The headline 'outperforms by over 20%' is relative to the base Qwen2.5VL model, which is a much weaker comparison; the abstract's framing could overstate the advance.

Human expert evaluation is thin: only 3 raters on 100 dialogues, and while κ = 0.79 and p < 0.05 are reported, per-model confidence intervals and the exact statistical test are not given. The CSR metric in the error-injection experiment is evaluated 'via manual evaluation' without describing who evaluated, blinding, or inter-rater reliability.

User study protocol details are missing: how the 200 participants were allocated across the seven compared systems (within- vs between-subjects), exposure duration, and whether ratings were counterbalanced are not reported, limiting interpretability of Table 4.

Modest methodological novelty relative to the system scope: the core techniques (persona-driven multi-agent simulation, LLM-generated teaching data, rubric-anchored GRPO with vetoes) are combinations of existing ideas (SocraticLM, TutorRL, rubric RL); the paper's value is largely in the careful instantiation for a new one-to-many clinical setting rather than new alignment methods.

Minor presentation/consistency issues: the veto set is stated as {CS-1, CS-2, IS-1} in Eq. 2 but Appendix C also describes a -15.0 penalty on IS-1/CS-1/CS-2 with slightly different wording; Figure 24's caption duplicates Figure 23's ('analysis quality judgment' though it is the clinical accuracy prompt); 'Gemini 3 Pro' and some cited works (e.g., He et al., 2026b; Ma et al., 2026) appear anachronistic/unverifiable, which weakens confidence in citation hygiene.
